summary: Introduces a syntax for defining feature sets formed from combinations and relations involving individual media features, such as saying a device supports one thing and either of two others. It was updated by RFC 2738 and RFC 2938.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2533 defines a common syntax for describing media features that a sender, recipient, or file format can handle. It also gives a procedure for checking whether two descriptions have any acceptable combination in common.

subtitle: A Boolean syntax for describing media capabilities and testing whether two descriptions overlap.

tldr.problem: Content negotiation needs a way to describe combinations of media features that senders, recipients, or file formats can handle.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2533 represents feature sets as Boolean predicates over feature tags and values. It defines a matching procedure that simplifies the combined predicates and checks whether any valid combination remains.
tldr.outcome: The syntax can describe capabilities and preferences, and the matching procedure determines whether two feature sets overlap. RFC 2533 was updated by RFC 2738 and RFC 2938.

facts.label: Matching normal form
facts.value: Disjunction of conjunctions, at most 3 levels

today: RFC 2533 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 2738 and RFC 2938. Read those documents with this syntax specification.

sections.title: Why Describe Media Feature Sets
sections.content:
Internet application protocols that negotiate content need to describe which media features a sender, recipient, or transmission format can handle. Individual feature tags and their registration process are defined separately in RFC 2506.

This document defines a syntax for combining feature tags and values into feature sets. It also describes an algorithm for matching two feature sets. The same expression form can describe a sender, a recipient, or a file format.
sections.plainLanguage: A content sender and receiver need a shared way to describe the media formats they can handle. This document supplies that syntax and a method for comparing two descriptions.

sections.title: Collections, Sets, and Predicates
sections.content:
A feature collection contains media feature tags and associated values. It can describe a specific rendering of a resource for a recipient. A feature set contains zero or more feature collections.

A feature set predicate is a function that tests a collection and returns TRUE or FALSE. TRUE means that the collection belongs to the set described by the predicate. Descriptions begin with all possible collections and apply constraints that remove unacceptable ones.

Feature values may be Boolean, enumerated, text, or numeric. Equality comparisons apply to all these values; less-than and greater-than comparisons apply to numeric and ordered values.
sections.plainLanguage: A feature collection describes one possible version of a resource. A predicate tests that version against rules and says whether it belongs in the set of acceptable versions.

sections.title: Writing Feature Predicates
sections.content:
The text syntax is based on LDAP search filters. A filter is written in parentheses, and its components can be joined with logical AND, OR, or NOT. A simple comparison tests a feature tag against a value with =, <=, or >=.

  • (& f1 f2) requires both predicates to be true.
  • (| f1 f2) requires at least one predicate to be true.
  • (! f1) requires the predicate to be false.
  • (tag=value) compares one feature with a value.

Set notation is shorthand for comparisons. For example, a list of acceptable values can be expanded into an OR of equality tests. Quality values from 0 to 1 can rank preferences, with a default of 1. This document gives no general rule for combining quality values from different parts of an expression.
sections.plainLanguage: The syntax combines feature tests with AND, OR, and NOT. A quality value can rank an option, but this document does not define how to combine separate preference scores.

sections.title: Feature Values and Units
sections.content:
A feature value may be Boolean, numeric, a token, or a quoted string. Numeric values can be integers or rationals, such as 3/2. The sign of a rational, if present, comes before the entire value.

Each feature tag has a standard unit. Values in that unit do not need a unit designation; an alternate unit can be written after the number. During matching, values with different unit designators are treated as different features. Applications should use a consistent unit for each feature.

The framework does not define comparison behavior for every possible data type. For example, comparisons for multi-part version strings are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Feature values can be yes or no, numbers, tokens, or text. If a number uses a non-standard unit, the expression names that unit so the comparison is clear.

sections.title: Checking Whether Feature Sets Match
sections.content:
To test two feature sets, the procedure combines their predicates with AND and asks whether any feature collection can satisfy the result. It first rewrites shorthand sets as simple comparisons and moves negations directly onto comparisons.

Next, the combined predicate is converted to disjunctive normal form: an OR of conjunctions. Each conjunction is grouped by feature tag. The comparison rules then merge constraints for each tag. If a conjunction contains contradictory constraints, it cannot match and is removed.

The feature sets overlap if at least one conjunction remains satisfiable. Selecting one final option based on quality values or other preferences is outside this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The matcher combines both descriptions, then removes combinations that contradict themselves. If at least one possible combination remains, the two feature sets overlap.

sections.title: Reusable Predicates and Security
sections.content:
A named predicate gives a reusable expression a name and may give it formal parameters. This document defines auxiliary predicates, which are attached to a filter in a where ... end block. Their names are visible within the filter body, but not to one another, and recursive predicates are not permitted.

For matching, a named predicate is replaced by its definition before conversion to disjunctive normal form. The RFC's security section warns that announced capabilities and preferences may reveal private information, incorrect capability data may disrupt operation, and capability queries may help identify hosts with known weaknesses.

Automatically answering queries from unknown systems is a particular concern. Directory services may be less problematic when proper authentication is available. Format-converting gateways can also interfere with message integrity and authenticity checks.
sections.plainLanguage: Repeated feature rules can be given a name and reused, as long as they do not call themselves. Capability information can reveal details or be misused, so systems should consider who can request or change it.
